title: West Sikkim on a Budget: What Things Really Cost
meta_description: Real 2025–26 costs for Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla and Namchi: shared jeeps, rooms, homestays, food, entries and guides, plus three daily budgets.
summary: West and South Sikkim can be done on ₹1,500–2,000 a person a day if you ride shared jeeps, stay in small hotels or village homestays and eat thalis. Reserved cars and peak-season rooms are what push budgets up. Here are indicative 2025–26 prices, three daily budgets and the places people quietly overspend.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: We get asked one question more than any other: how cheap can Pelling and Yuksom really be? Cheaper than most people expect. The road network of Gyalshing, Soreng and Namchi districts runs on shared jeeps, the Sumos and Boleros that leave each town when they fill, and a seat costs a fraction of a reserved car. Rooms in Pelling start around ₹1,200 a night outside the October and May rush, and a village homestay gives you a bed, dinner and breakfast for ₹1,500–2,500 a person.

The money goes on three things: hiring a private car for every hop, booking a Pelling hotel at the last minute in Puja or summer holidays, and paying package prices for a list of sightseeing points you could reach on foot or by shared jeep. Avoid those three and a week here costs less than a long weekend in many hill towns. All figures below are indicative for 2025–26; fares and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Getting around: jeeps and cars
paras: Jorethang is the hub for the south and west, and Geyzing (Gyalshing), about 10 km below Pelling, is the hub for the west. Shared jeeps run from early morning, most leave before noon, and the last ones on quieter routes may go by 1 pm. Book a seat at the counter the evening before if you can. The front seat beside the driver is usually the same price and the best view.
list: Two people with bags often pay less for three or four shared seats than for one reserved car.
A reserved car makes sense for a family of four doing Pelling to Yuksom with stops at Khecheopalri and the falls.
Fares rise in peak weeks and after fuel price changes; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Rooms, homestays and trekkers' huts
paras: Pelling has the widest choice. Upper Pelling has the views and the budget lodges, including long-running places such as Hotel Garuda, and Lower Pelling is quieter. Budget rooms run ₹1,200–2,500 a night for two, mid-range hotels ₹3,000–6,000. Prices can double in the first half of October, around Christmas and in May, and fall sharply from June to September and in January and February.

Village homestays are the better deal and the better story. At Hee Bermiok, Dentam, Uttarey, Kaluk, Rinchenpong, Okhrey below Barsey and Kewzing near Ravangla, families charge about ₹1,500–2,500 a person including a home-cooked dinner and breakfast. That usually means dal, rice, a seasonal green, pickle made with dalle khursani chilli, sometimes churpi or local chicken. Yangsum Heritage Farm at Rinchenpong sits at the comfortable end of this scale.

On the Goecha La trail the government trekkers' huts at Tshoka and Dzongri are basic and cheap, but most trekkers book through an agency that supplies tents and a cook. At Barsey the Guras Kunj trekkers' hut is the simple option inside the sanctuary.

Out of season, ask for the rate before you look at the room, then ask again for a two- or three-night price. In July or January a ₹2,500 Pelling room often goes for ₹1,500, and many homestays round down for families. Check whether hot water is from a geyser or a bucket, and whether the view room costs extra; in Upper Pelling it usually does, and on a clear November morning it is worth it.

sections.heading: Food, entries and small costs
paras: A veg or non-veg thali in Pelling, Namchi or Ravangla costs ₹150–250, often with free refills of rice and dal. A plate of momos is ₹80–150, a bowl of thukpa or thenthuk a little more, and roadside tea ₹20–30. Eating where the jeep drivers eat, near the Geyzing and Jorethang stands, is reliably cheap and filling.

Monastery and park entries are small: usually ₹20–100 at places such as Pemayangtse, Rabdentse, the Samdruptse statue in Namchi, Char Dham and the Ravangla Buddha Park. The glass skywalk at the Chenrezig statue near Pelling has its own ticket. Some sites and towns charge an eco or entry levy, and Sikkim has restricted packaged drinking water in some areas, so carry a bottle you can refill. Check current status before you travel.

Homestay rates include dinner and breakfast, so on those days you only pay for lunch and tea. Budget ₹500–700 a person a day for food if you eat simply in towns, and remember that hotel restaurants in Pelling charge noticeably more than the small family eateries on the main road. A packet of local biscuits and a flask of tea from your hotel saves money on long jeep days.

sections.heading: Guides, porters and trekking
paras: A licensed guide is mandatory on the Dzongri and Goecha La trek, and Khangchendzonga National Park permits are issued at the forest office in Yuksom. Indicative day rates are ₹1,500–2,500 for a guide and ₹800–1,200 for a porter, plus food and park fees. Foreign nationals must go through a registered agency, in a group, with a Restricted Area Permit. Rules and fees change most seasons, so check current status before you travel.
Shorter walks cost nothing beyond a tip: the steep 45 minutes from Yuksom to Dubdi Monastery, the forest path to Rabdentse, the ridge walk up to Sanga Choeling, and the 4 km from Hilley to Barsey.

For Barsey, Maenam Hill and the Singshore Bridge walk, a local guide is optional; homestays can usually find someone from the village for a few hundred rupees and a meal, which also keeps the money in the village.

paras: These are per person, per day, for two people sharing, excluding the journey from Siliguri.

sections.heading: A sample week for two
paras: Here is how a seven-night loop from Siliguri works out for two people on a value budget, using shared jeeps for the long legs and one reserved car day. Figures are indicative for 2025–26; check current status before you travel.
list: Night 1–2, Pelling: shared jeeps via Jorethang about ₹900 for two; budget hotel ₹2,000 a night; walks to Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling with small entries.
Night 3–4, Yuksom: shared jeep about ₹400 for two; simple guesthouse ₹1,500–2,000; Norbugang, Kathok Lake and Dubdi on foot.
Night 5, Hee Bermiok or Dentam homestay: reserved car day via Khecheopalri about ₹3,000; homestay with meals about ₹4,000 for two.
Night 6–7, Ravangla and Namchi: jeeps via Legship and Jorethang about ₹600 for two; rooms ₹1,500–2,500; Buddha Park, Samdruptse and Char Dham.
Return: Namchi to Siliguri by shared jeep about ₹600 for two.
Total: roughly ₹26,000–30,000 for two, or ₹13,000–15,000 each, with meals.

sections.heading: Where people overspend
list: Booking a reserved car from NJP for one or two people when direct shared jeeps to Pelling or Jorethang leave from Siliguri each morning.
Buying a ten-point Pelling sightseeing package when Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling are walks from Upper Pelling.
Arriving in Pelling in the first half of October or in May without a booking and taking whatever room is left.
Hiring a car for the day just for Khecheopalri, when a shared jeep to the lake or Yuksom and a walk does the job.
Paying for bottled water instead of refilling at hotels and homestays.
Doing Pelling, Ravangla and Namchi as separate return trips from Siliguri instead of one loop via Jorethang.

faqs.q: How much does a 5-day trip to Pelling and Yuksom cost?
faqs.a: On a shoestring, about ₹8,000–11,000 a person for five days with shared jeeps from Siliguri, budget rooms or homestays and simple meals. A value trip with one reserved sightseeing day and homestay nights runs ₹15,000–22,000 a person. A comfort trip with a car most days and mid-range hotels runs ₹30,000–45,000. All figures are indicative for 2025–26 and exclude travel to Siliguri.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to reach Pelling from Siliguri?
faqs.a: A direct shared jeep from the Siliguri stands near the SNT terminus costs about ₹450–600 a seat and takes 5–6 hours, but there are only a few, mostly in the morning. Otherwise take a jeep to Jorethang for ₹250–350 and another to Pelling for ₹150–220. Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is a homestay in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Most village homestays in Hee Bermiok, Dentam, Uttarey, Kaluk, Rinchenpong, Okhrey and Kewzing charge about ₹1,500–2,500 a person a night with dinner and breakfast. Children usually pay less, and some families give a better rate for three or more nights. Prices are indicative for 2025–26 and rise a little in October and May.

faqs.q: How much does a reserved car cost for Pelling sightseeing?
faqs.a: A small car for a day of Pelling sightseeing usually costs ₹2,500–3,500 in 2025–26, covering points such as Khecheopalri Lake, Rimbi and Kanchenjunga Falls, and sometimes Yuksom. Larger vehicles cost more. Agree the list of stops and the finishing time before you leave, and check current status before you travel as rates rise in peak weeks.

faqs.q: Are monasteries in West Sikkim free to enter?
faqs.a: Many working gompas ask only for a donation, while better-known sites charge small tickets, usually ₹20–100. Pemayangtse, the Rabdentse ruins, the Ravangla Buddha Park, Samdruptse and Char Dham in Namchi all have modest fees, and cameras may cost extra inside some prayer halls. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a guide for Goecha La cost?
faqs.a: Independent licensed guides charge roughly ₹1,500–2,500 a day and porters ₹800–1,200 a day, plus their food, park permits and camping costs. Most people book through a Yuksom or Siliguri agency that bundles guide, cook, tents and permits per person. Foreigners must use a registered agency. Rules and fees change; check current status before you travel.

Room rates are lowest from June to September, during the monsoon, and in January and February, when nights are cold. Many Pelling hotels discount 30–50 percent in those months. The catch is weather: monsoon landslides can block roads for hours or days, and views of Kanchenjunga are rare in the rains. Late November and early December are a good compromise.

faqs.q: Can I visit Pelling without a car?
faqs.a: Yes. Upper Pelling is compact, and Pemayangtse Monastery, the Rabdentse ruins and Sanga Choeling are all walks from town. Shared jeeps from Pelling and Geyzing reach Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Dentam and Jorethang. The only drawback is timing: most jeeps leave in the morning, so plan a single destination for each day.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Carry enough cash for several days. Pelling, Geyzing, Jorethang, Namchi and Ravangla have ATMs, but they sometimes run dry in peak weeks, and mobile signal for UPI is patchy in villages such as Uttarey and Hee Bermiok. Shared jeeps, small eateries and many homestays prefer cash, though more of them now accept UPI.
